_note: Name-facts for Vietnam (FT-41, docs/PLAN_V0.9.md). See italy.json for
Vietnamese province names are Sino-Vietnamese compounds, and the same
handful of characters build most of the sixty-three:
bac = north    nam = south    dong = east    tay = west
thai/thanh = peaceful, clear   binh = peace   an = safe, peaceful
ha = river     giang = river   hai = sea      son = mountain
long = dragon  quang = broad   phu = rich     tho = longevity
ninh = tranquil   hoa = harmony   lam = forest   dinh = settled
So Hai Phong is 'coastal defence', Ha Noi 'inside the rivers', Quang
Ninh 'broad tranquillity', Ha Long 'descending dragon'. A minority
come from Tai, Cham or Khmer and are flagged where they do.
WATCH THE IDS. slugify drops the Vietnamese diacritics and eats a
leading D-with-stroke, so Dien Bien is 'ien-bien', Da Nang is 'a-nang'
and Dong Nai is 'ong-nai'. That is the documented slugify limitation
in mapBuildUtils.ts, deliberately not 'fixed' because ids key saved
ha-giang: "River Giang" — ha and giang are both river words, one Sino-Vietnamese, one older.
The Dong Van karst plateau here is a UNESCO geopark of limestone spires, and the Ma Pi Leng pass is the most spectacular road in the country.
It is Vietnam's northernmost province and one of its most ethnically diverse, with Hmong, Tay, Dao and Lo Lo communities.
cao-bang: Ho Chi Minh returned from thirty years abroad to the Pac Bo cave here in 1941, and the revolution was organised from it.
Ban Gioc on its Chinese border is the largest waterfall in south-east Asia that sits on an international boundary.
lai-chau: From a Tai name; chau was an administrative district in the old highland system.
One of the poorest and least populated provinces, almost entirely mountain.
Its Fansipan foothills and the Tam Duong valley grow tea, and the White Thai and Hmong are the largest groups.
lao-cai: From Chinese lao jie, "old market" — the border trading post the town grew from.
Sapa here was built as a French hill station and is now the most visited highland town in Vietnam.
Fansipan, at 3,147 m the highest mountain in Indochina, is in this province and now has a cable car to the summit.
bac-kan: "Northern Kan" — bac is north, a prefix on a dozen Vietnamese names.
Ba Be lake in it is the largest natural lake in Vietnam, held in limestone and surrounded by forest.
The least populated province in the country.
tuyen-quang: "Proclaimed brightness" — quang is broad or bright, and tuyen to declare.
The Viet Minh's wartime capital was here at Tan Trao, where the August Revolution was launched in 1945.
Its Na Hang reserve holds one of the last populations of the Tonkin snub-nosed monkey, found only in Vietnam.
lang-son: "Mountain pass" — lang a village or pass, son mountain.
The Friendship Pass here has been the main land gate to China for two thousand years, and armies have used it in both directions.
The 1979 Chinese invasion destroyed the town almost completely; it was rebuilt from nothing.
yen-bai: "Peaceful Bai" — yen means peaceful or safe, one of the commonest elements in Vietnamese names.
The Mu Cang Chai rice terraces here are a national monument, cut by Hmong farmers into slopes too steep for machines.
The 1930 Yen Bai mutiny against the French was crushed and its leaders guillotined, which pushed the independence movement towards communism.
ien-bien: "Border administration" — the name of a garrison town on the Lao frontier.
Dien Bien Phu here is where the Viet Minh beat the French in 1954, ending colonial rule in Indochina.
The Vietnamese dragged artillery over mountains by hand to positions the French thought impossible, which decided the battle.
thai-nguyen: "Clear source" or "peaceful plain" — thai meaning great or peaceful, nguyen a source or plain.
Its tan cuong tea is the most prized green tea in Vietnam.
It was the site of the country's first integrated steelworks, built with Chinese help in the 1960s.
bac-giang: "Northern river" — north of the Cau river.
It grows more lychees than any other province, and the Luc Ngan harvest is a national event.
The Yen Tu range on its border holds the Truc Lam Buddhist sect's mountain monasteries, founded by a king who abdicated to become a monk.
vinh-phuc: "Eternal happiness" — vinh eternal, phuc happiness or blessing.
Tam Dao in it was another French hill station, at 900 m with a cool climate an hour from Hanoi.
It is one of the most industrialised northern provinces, with Honda and Toyota plants.
phu-tho: "Rich and long-lived" — phu rich, tho longevity.
The Hung kings, the legendary founders of Vietnam, are said to have ruled from here, and their temple hosts the national ancestral festival.
Xoan singing from this province is on the UNESCO intangible heritage list.
son-la: "Mountain La" — son mountain, La the river.
The Son La dam is the largest hydroelectric plant in south-east Asia.
The French prison here held Vietnamese political prisoners including several future leaders, and is now a museum.
quang-ninh: Ha Long Bay is here — "descending dragon", from a legend of dragons spitting jewels that became the 1,600 limestone islands.
It holds most of Vietnam's coal, mined since the French period, and the province borders China.
bac-ninh: The smallest province in Vietnam by area, and the most densely populated after the cities.
Quan ho, its call-and-response love duets sung between villages, is a UNESCO heritage item, and Samsung's largest phone factories are here.
ha-noi: "Inside the rivers" — ha river, noi inside: the city sits in the bend of the Red River.
It has been a capital on and off since 1010, when a king saw a dragon rise and named it Thang Long, ascending dragon.
Its Temple of Literature, founded in 1070, was Vietnam's first university, and the names of its doctoral graduates are carved on stone tortoises.
hai-duong: "Sea ocean" or "eastern sea" — hai sea, duong ocean.
Its green bean cake, banh dau xanh, is the standard gift brought back from the province.
Chu Dau pottery from here was exported across Asia in the 1400s, and a wreck off the coast recovered 240,000 pieces.
hung-yen: "Flourishing peace" — hung to flourish, yen peaceful.
Pho Hien here was a major international port in the 1600s, with Dutch, Japanese and Chinese quarters — the saying ran "first Kinh Ky, second Pho Hien".
The river silted up and the port died, which is why an inland farming province was once Vietnam's second city.
hai-phong: "Coastal defence" — hai sea, phong to guard.
The third largest city and the main port of the north.
Cat Ba island off it holds the golden-headed langur, of which about 70 remain — one of the rarest primates in the world.
hoa-binh: The Hoabinhian culture is named after this province: stone tools found here defined a whole prehistoric period across south-east Asia.
It is the heartland of the Muong people, whose language is the closest living relative of Vietnamese.
ha-nam: "South of the river" — ha river, nam south.
Tam Chuc in it is one of the largest Buddhist complexes in the world by area.
It is a small delta province, almost entirely rice, an hour south of Hanoi.
thai-binh: "Great peace" — a name that has been used for the region since the eleventh century.
Entirely flat delta with no mountains and no forest, and among the most intensively farmed land in Asia.
It has the highest rice yield per hectare in Vietnam and sends migrant workers all over the country.
nam-inh: "Southern settlement" — nam south, dinh a settled place.
It was the capital of the Tran dynasty, which beat three Mongol invasions in the 1200s, once by planting iron-tipped stakes in a riverbed.
Phat Diem cathedral nearby is built in Vietnamese temple style with curved roofs, and the province has the country's largest Catholic population.
ninh-binh: Trang An here is a UNESCO site of limestone towers and river caves, and Hoa Lu was Vietnam's capital in the tenth century.
It is called Ha Long Bay on land, and the caves are rowed through by boatwomen using their feet on the oars.
thanh-hoa: "Pure harmony" — thanh clear or pure, hoa harmony.
The Dong Son culture, which made Vietnam's great bronze drums from about 600 BC, is named after a village in this province.
The Ho dynasty citadel here, built in 1397 from enormous stone blocks, is a UNESCO site.
nghe-an: "Peaceful Nghe" — an, peace, on an older regional name.
Ho Chi Minh was born here in 1890, in a village of thatched houses now preserved.
The largest province in Vietnam by area, running from the sea to the Lao border.
ha-tinh: Nguyen Du, who wrote the Tale of Kieu — the poem every Vietnamese can quote — was from here.
The Ke Go reserve holds several bird species found nowhere else, and the province was the site of a major 2016 industrial marine pollution disaster.
quang-binh: Son Doong in it is the largest cave passage in the world, big enough to hold a New York block, with its own jungle and clouds inside.
The province is only 50 km wide at Vietnam's narrowest point, and the Ho Chi Minh trail ran through its mountains.
quang-tri: The seventeenth parallel ran through it, so this province was the Demilitarised Zone dividing Vietnam from 1954 to 1975.
The Vinh Moc tunnels here sheltered a whole village underground for six years, with a maternity room where seventeen children were born.
thua-thien-hue: Hue is probably a worn-down form of Thuan Hoa, the old regional name; thua thien means "receiving heaven".
Hue was the imperial capital from 1802 to 1945, and its citadel and tombs are a UNESCO site.
Its court music, nha nhac, is another UNESCO heritage item, and the city's cuisine is the most refined in Vietnam.
a-nang: Probably from Cham daknan, "big river mouth" — one of the Cham names that survive along this coast.
The Marble Mountains here are five limestone hills named for the five elements, honeycombed with caves and shrines.
The first American combat troops in Vietnam landed on its beach in 1965, and the city is now the country's most liveable by common consent.
quang-nam: "Broad south" — the southern expansion of the Vietnamese state into Cham territory.
Hoi An in it was an international port from the 1500s and is preserved almost intact as a UNESCO site.
My Son nearby is a complex of Cham Hindu temples built between the 4th and 14th centuries, also UNESCO-listed.
quang-ngai: The My Lai massacre took place here in 1968, and the site is a memorial.
Ly Son island off its coast grows garlic in sand carried up from the beach, and was a base for the Hoang Sa flotilla that claimed the Paracels.
kon-tum: From Bahnar: kon means village and tum a lake — "the village by the lake".
One of the most ethnically diverse provinces, with Bahnar, Sedang, Gia Rai and Gie Trieng communities.
Its wooden cathedral, built by the French in 1913 in local stilt-house style, is one of the most unusual churches in Asia.
binh-inh: "Pacified and settled" — binh peace, dinh settled: a name given after the region was taken from Champa.
The Tay Son brothers, who overthrew both ruling houses and briefly united Vietnam in the 1780s, came from here.
Its Cham towers at Banh It and Duong Long are among the best preserved anywhere.
gia-lai: From the Jarai people, whose name the Vietnamese wrote as Gia Rai.
Pleiku in it was a key base in the central highlands war, and the 1975 retreat from it began the collapse of South Vietnam.
Bien Ho, a crater lake, supplies the city's water, and the province grows coffee, pepper and rubber.
phu-yen: "Rich and peaceful" — phu rich, yen peaceful.
Its Ganh Da Dia is a field of interlocking basalt columns on the shore, like the Giant's Causeway.
It has the easternmost point of mainland Vietnam at Mui Dien, so it sees the sunrise first.
ak-lak: From Rade: dak means water and lak is a lake — "the water of Lak".
Buon Ma Thuot here is the coffee capital of Vietnam, and Vietnam is the world's largest producer of robusta.
The gong culture of the central highlands, centred on this province, is a UNESCO heritage item.
khanh-hoa: Nha Trang in it has the best-known beach in Vietnam and a Cham tower complex, Po Nagar, still used for worship.
Its swiftlet nests, harvested from sea caves for bird's nest soup, were a royal monopoly and are still among the most expensive foods in the world.
ak-nong: From Mnong: dak water again, plus the M'Nong people's name.
Its volcanic cave system at Krong No is the longest lava tube system in south-east Asia, found only in 2007.
Split from Dak Lak in 2004, and it grows coffee, pepper and cashews on basalt soil.
binh-phuoc: Its Bu Gia Map park is one of the last lowland forests in southern Vietnam.
It produces most of Vietnam's cashews, and Vietnam is the world's largest cashew exporter.
lam-ong: "Forest of the Dong" — lam forest, plus the Da Dong river.
Da Lat in it was built by the French as a hill station at 1,500 m and still grows Europe's vegetables and flowers for the whole country.
Its cool climate makes it Vietnam's honeymoon city, and the province produces almost all the country's artichokes and strawberries.
ninh-thuan: The driest province in Vietnam, with cactus, salt pans and vineyards — the only place in the country that grows table grapes commercially.
It has the largest remaining Cham population, who still keep their own Hindu and Bani Muslim traditions and their own new year, Kate.
tay-ninh: The Cao Dai religion was founded here in 1926 and its Great Temple canonises Victor Hugo, Sun Yat-sen and Joan of Arc among its saints.
Ba Den mountain rises 986 m straight out of the plain, the only relief for a hundred kilometres.
binh-duong: The most industrialised province in Vietnam, with the highest income per head of any province.
Its lacquerware and pottery villages supplied Saigon for two centuries before the factories arrived.
binh-thuan: Mui Ne here has red and white sand dunes, and the steady wind makes it a kitesurfing centre.
It grows nearly all of Vietnam's dragon fruit, grown on posts under lights that are switched on at night to force flowering.
ong-nai: "Deer river" — nai is a deer, and the Dong Nai is southern Vietnam's longest internal river.
Cat Tien park in it holds one of the last lowland tropical forests and was where Vietnam's last Javan rhino was killed in 2010.
It is one of the country's industrial heartlands, and its Bien Hoa was a major American airbase.
thanh-pho-ho-chi-minh: "Ho Chi Minh City" — renamed in 1976; the older name Saigon may be from Khmer prey nokor, "forest city", and is still what people say.
The largest city in Vietnam and its economic engine, producing about a fifth of national GDP.
The Cu Chi tunnels outside it run 250 km, with kitchens, hospitals and workshops, dug by hand and fought over for years.
long-an: The gateway from Ho Chi Minh City into the Mekong delta.
Its Dong Thap Muoi, the Plain of Reeds, is acid sulphate wetland that took decades of engineering to farm.
ong-thap: "Eastern tower" or "Thap's field" — dong can be field or east, thap a tower.
Tram Chim park here protects the sarus crane, the tallest flying bird in the world, which winters on its wetlands.
Its Sa Dec flower village supplies the delta, and Marguerite Duras set The Lover in the town.
ba-ria-vung-tau: Vung Tau is "anchorage bay"; Ba Ria is said to be named for a woman who cleared the land in the 1700s.
Vietnam's offshore oil and gas comes ashore here, and the province has long had the highest GDP per head outside the cities.
The French called Vung Tau Cap Saint-Jacques, and it was Saigon's seaside resort.
an-giang: Oc Eo in it was the port of Funan, a kingdom of the first centuries AD, and Roman coins have been dug up there.
It has the largest Cham Muslim and Khmer populations in the delta, and the Sam mountain pilgrimage draws millions.
tien-giang: "Front river" — the northern branch of the Mekong, as opposed to the Hau, the rear river.
My Tho, its capital, was founded by Chinese refugees in the 1680s and is the oldest city in the delta.
Its floating markets and fruit orchards are the delta's standard day trip from Ho Chi Minh City.
can-tho: Possibly from cam thi giang, "river of poems", or from a Khmer word — the derivation is contested.
The largest city in the Mekong delta and its administrative centre.
Cai Rang floating market here is the biggest in the region; boats advertise what they sell by hanging a sample from a pole.
vinh-long: It sits between the two main Mekong branches, so it is almost entirely orchard and rice.
Its brick kilns along the Co Chien river form a landscape of beehive chimneys, now disappearing.
ben-tre: From a Khmer name, possibly srok treay, "fish region", reinterpreted in Vietnamese as "bamboo wharf".
The coconut province: it has more coconut palms than anywhere in Vietnam, and makes candy, oil and fibre from them.
The 1960 Ben Tre uprising was the start of the armed insurgency in the south.
kien-giang: "Establishing river" — kien to build or establish.
Phu Quoc island belongs to it — Vietnam's largest island, closer to Cambodia than to the mainland, and the source of the country's best fish sauce.
Ha Tien on its coast was an autonomous Chinese-run port state in the 1700s.
hau-giang: "Rear river" — the southern branch of the Mekong, paired with Tien Giang.
Split from Can Tho in 2004, and almost entirely rice and fruit.
Its Lung Ngoc Hoang reserve is one of the last pieces of undrained delta swamp forest.
tra-vinh: From Khmer prha trapeang, "sacred pond" — one of the clearest Khmer survivals in the delta.
It has one of the largest Khmer Krom populations in Vietnam, and about 140 Khmer Theravada pagodas.
Its Ba Om pond and the ancient trees around it are a national monument.
soc-trang: From Khmer srok kh'leang, "the region of the storehouse".
The Doi pagoda here is home to thousands of flying foxes that roost in its trees and are protected by the monks.
Its Khmer ngo boat races draw crews of fifty paddlers and tens of thousands of spectators.
bac-lieu: Probably from a Khmer or Chinese name for a place of salt flats.
The Bac Lieu prince, who famously burned banknotes to boil an egg for a bet, is the delta's standard story about colonial-era excess.
It has the largest wind farm in Vietnam, built out into the tidal flats.
ca-mau: From Khmer tuk khmau, "black water" — the tannin-stained water of its mangrove swamps.
The southernmost province: Vietnam's mainland ends at its cape, which is still growing seaward as the Mekong deposits silt.
Its U Minh Ha forest is one of the last peat swamp forests in south-east Asia.
viet-tri: "Viet pond" or "Viet place" — one of the oldest recorded settlements in the country.
The Hung kings are said to have had their capital here, and the national ancestral temple is just outside.
It was built up as an industrial city in the 1950s with Chinese and Soviet help.
son-tay: Its citadel of 1822 is built of laterite and is one of the best preserved in the north.
An American raid on its prison camp in 1970 found no prisoners; they had been moved.
cam-pha: Probably from a local name; the town sits on the Ha Long coast.
It is the centre of Vietnam’s open-cast coal mining, with terraced pits above the sea.
Its coal has been dug since the French opened the field in the 1880s.
ha-long: "Descending dragon" — from the legend of dragons spitting jewels that became the bay’s islands.
Those 1,600 limestone islands are a UNESCO site and Vietnam’s best-known landscape.
The town was called Hon Gai until 1994, when it took the bay’s name for tourism.
vinh: Possibly from a word for a gulf or an older local name.
It was flattened by American bombing — one of the most heavily hit cities in the north — and rebuilt with East German help.
Ho Chi Minh was born in a village just outside it.
ong-hoi: "Eastern gathering" — dong east, hoi to gather.
The Son Doong and Phong Nha caves are in its province, the largest cave passages in the world.
It sits at Vietnam’s narrowest point, where the country is about 50 km wide.
hue: Probably a worn-down form of Thuan Hoa, the old regional name.
It was the imperial capital from 1802 to 1945; its citadel and royal tombs are a UNESCO site.
The 1968 battle for the city was the longest and bloodiest of the Tet Offensive.
pleiku: From Jarai: plei means village, and Ku was a local leader.
It was a key base in the central highlands, and the 1975 retreat from it began the fall of South Vietnam.
Bien Ho, a crater lake beside the town, supplies its water.
quy-nhon: From an old name meaning something like "returning to benevolence".
It was a Cham port, and Cham towers still stand within the city.
Its ICISE science centre hosts international physics meetings, founded by a Vietnamese-French physicist.
buon-ma-thuot: From Rade: buon means village, and Ma Thuot was a chief — "the village of father Thuot".
The coffee capital of Vietnam, and Vietnam is the world’s largest producer of robusta.
Its capture in March 1975 was the opening move of the offensive that ended the war six weeks later.
nha-trang: From Cham ea trang, "reed river" — one of the Cham names that survive along this coast.
Its Po Nagar towers, built by the Cham from the 700s, are still used for worship.
Alexandre Yersin, who identified the plague bacterium, lived and is buried here, and is revered locally.
a-lat: From K'Ho da lat, "the river of the Lat people" — the French also liked the Latin motto they could make of the letters.
Built as a French hill station at 1,500 m, it still grows Europe’s vegetables and flowers for the country.
Its cool climate makes it Vietnam’s honeymoon city, and it grows almost all the country’s artichokes.
cam-ranh: Of local origin; the bay is one of the finest deep-water harbours in Asia.
The Russian fleet anchored here before sailing to its destruction at Tsushima in 1905.
It was a major American base and then a Soviet one, and is now Vietnam’s tourist airport for Nha Trang.
phan-rang-thap-cham: Phan Rang is from Cham Panduranga; Thap Cham means "Cham tower".
The Po Klong Garai towers above it are the best preserved Cham temples in Vietnam.
The driest place in the country, with cactus, salt pans and table grapes.
bien-hoa: "Peaceful frontier" — bien a border, hoa harmony.
One of the oldest Vietnamese settlements in the south, founded by Chinese refugees in the 1600s.
Its airbase was the busiest in the world at points during the war, and is heavily dioxin-contaminated.
thu-dau-mot: From a phrase about a tree on a mound — the derivation is debated.
Its lacquerware and pottery villages supplied Saigon for two centuries.
It is the capital of Binh Duong, the province with the highest income per head in Vietnam.
phan-thiet: From Cham hamu lithit, a local place name.
It makes the most famous fish sauce in Vietnam, fermented in wooden vats along the shore.
Mui Ne beside it has red and white sand dunes and is a kitesurfing centre.
ho-chi-minh: Renamed in 1976 for Ho Chi Minh; the older Saigon may be from Khmer prey nokor, "forest city".
The largest city in Vietnam, producing about a fifth of national GDP.
The Cu Chi tunnels outside it run 250 km, with kitchens, hospitals and workshops dug by hand.
tan-an: The gateway from Ho Chi Minh City into the Mekong delta.
Its Dong Thap Muoi, the Plain of Reeds, took decades of engineering to make farmable.
cao-lanh: From an older local name, possibly honouring a woman called Lanh.
Tram Chim park nearby protects the sarus crane, the tallest flying bird in the world.
It sits on the Tien, the northern branch of the Mekong.
long-xuyen: It is the capital of An Giang, which has the delta’s largest Cham Muslim and Khmer populations.
Ton Duc Thang, who succeeded Ho Chi Minh as president, was born on an island opposite the town.
vung-tau: "Anchorage bay" — vung a bay, tau a ship.
The French called it Cap Saint-Jacques and made it Saigon’s seaside resort.
Vietnam’s offshore oil and gas comes ashore here, and a 32 m Christ statue stands over the cape.
my-tho: From a Khmer name, probably me sa, "white woman" or a local term, reinterpreted in Vietnamese.
Founded by Chinese refugees in the 1680s, it is the oldest city in the Mekong delta.
Hu tieu My Tho, its noodle soup, is one of the delta’s best-known dishes.
rach-gia: "Gia tree creek" — rach a creek, gia a mangrove-like tree.
Much of the modern town stands on land reclaimed from the sea.
It is the ferry port for Phu Quoc, Vietnam’s largest island.
